summary.central_question: With the trade deal collapsing and full U.S. tariffs looming, will China keep the yuan stable or let it weaken to offset the tariffs?
summary.main_thesis: China will likely limit near-term yuan weakness while it tests whether a deal is still possible, saving a major depreciation for after tariffs are fully extended.

content.text: With the trade deal collapsing and full U.S. tariffs looming, will China keep the yuan stable or let it weaken to offset the tariffs?
content.reason: A large trade shock forces a choice between holding the exchange rate and letting it absorb the shock.

passages.source_excerpt: Will China continue to want to keep its currency stable, or would it want to try to offset the (substantial) trade impact of “full” U.S. tariffs with a weaker yuan?

content.text: The deal's collapse may stem from China pulling back its offer, or from Trump deciding the deal was not great enough; Fickling suggests a deficit-fixated Trump may not want a deal at all.
content.reason: When negotiations break down, list the competing accounts of who moved before judging.

passages.source_excerpt: Maybe China really miscalculated and pulled back its offer during the negotiations in Beijing last week and thus provoked Trump’s tweet storm. Or perhaps Trump

content.text: Full tariffs would raise about $100–140 billion, roughly half a point of GDP fiscal tightening, smaller than the dollar's 2014–15 drag.
content.reason: Tariff revenue drains private spending just as a tax increase does.

passages.source_excerpt: putting 25 percent tariffs on close to $550 billion in imports would, if importers cannot substitute away from Chinese goods in the short-run, put something like $140 billion into the U.S. Treasury

content.text: The tariff fiscal drag is noticeable but not recessionary, partly offset by tax cuts and spending.
content.reason: A fiscal shock of under a percent of GDP rarely causes a recession alone, especially with offsetting stimulus.

passages.source_excerpt: That’s big enough to notice but, as Dr. Krugman notes, not big enough to generate a recession on its own.

content.text: UBS estimates full tariffs plus retaliation could cut China's growth by 1.5 points; exports to the U.S. are 3–4% of China's GDP.
content.reason: A country's exposure to a tariff scales with the share of its output sold to the taxing market.

passages.source_excerpt: UBS estimates that 25 percent tariffs on all of China’s exports to the United States, plus Chinese retaliation against U.S. imports, might knock 1.5 percentage points off China’s GDP growth

content.text: Beyond soybean cuts and tariff retaliation, currency depreciation is China's natural asymmetric response.
content.reason: A country facing tariffs can offset them by letting its currency fall, lowering its export prices.

passages.source_excerpt: But letting the yuan weaken has always been, in my view, the logical “asymmetric” Chinese response to a trade war.

content.text: Markets would push the yuan down, so stability requires active intervention, and depreciation requires eventually setting a new floor.
content.reason: Markets front-run expected currency moves, so a managed rate needs visible signals in either direction.

passages.source_excerpt: The market would certainly test China’s resolve—so if China didn’t want the yuan to weaken, it would need to take action—intervene, manage the fix, tighten controls

content.text: China has ample dollars at the central bank and banks to manage its currency either way.
content.reason: A country with large liquid foreign assets and limited net foreign debt can choose its exchange rate.

passages.source_excerpt: China has the firepower it needs to continue to manage its currency (concerns about China’s foreign currency debts are overstated in aggregate

content.text: Critics overstated the weakness of the deal's currency stability commitment, which locked in current policy and nudged China toward fiscal stimulus.
content.reason: A commitment matching existing policy is still valuable if it rules out a costly deviation.

passages.source_excerpt: Indeed, I thought much of the criticism of China’s reported commitment to currency stability in the (now aborted?) trade deal was overdone.

content.text: China's manufacturing surplus remains about $1 trillion, and a larger one would harm the world economy and fuel populism in left-behind regions.
content.reason: Large manufacturing surpluses export adjustment costs to trading partners' industrial regions.

passages.source_excerpt: China’s manufacturing surplus has stayed around $1 trillion even as its current account surplus has come down

content.text: A stable yuan has gone with a stable, balanced Chinese balance of payments.
content.reason: Exchange rate expectations drive private capital flows, so a credible peg damps outflow pressure.

passages.source_excerpt: as long as China’s currency stayed stable, its balance of payments, in my view, also would remain stable.

content.text: Reserves alone understate China's external activity; state bank lending abroad and bank borrowing matter more.
content.reason: Where state banks hold foreign assets, official reserves are an incomplete measure of official external activity.

passages.source_excerpt: But looking only at reserves misses the real action in China’s balance of payments these days.

content.text: Chinese bank lending abroad has soared for nine years, funded by bank borrowing and $150–200 billion of portfolio inflows, leaving state banks with large net foreign assets.
content.reason: Gross official-sector outflows can be financed by private inflows, keeping net positions balanced.

passages.source_excerpt: Every indicator I have found suggests the state banks now have a substantial (and growing) net foreign asset position.

content.text: BIS data on global banks' exposure to China broadly matches China's own figures.
content.reason: Cross-check a country's own statistics against counterparties' independent records.

passages.source_excerpt: The BIS data (which shows global banks exposure to China) isn’t that different from China’s own data.

content.text: Intervention proxies show two-way state bank activity, with no sustained pressure either way; trade surplus covers tourism and errors.
content.reason: Alternating purchases and sales of foreign currency indicate an equilibrium rather than a defended disequilibrium.

passages.source_excerpt: There have been months when China’s state banks have sold foreign currency, but also months when China’s state banks have bought.

content.text: Intervention by state banks, not just the central bank, is the relevant indicator of China's currency management.
content.reason: Official intervention can be done off the central bank's balance sheet through state-controlled institutions.

content.text: Recent stability supports two options: keep the yuan stable, or use control to engineer a managed depreciation.
content.reason: The same evidence of control can justify either holding steady or a controlled move.

passages.source_excerpt: Well, because it lends itself to two different interpretations of what China can and should do in response to the increase in U.S. tariffs.

content.text: Even if tariffs and oil sanctions push China into a current account deficit, a credible stable yuan would keep inflows coming and protect reserves.
content.reason: A small external deficit is easily financed when investors expect currency stability.

passages.source_excerpt: if China signaled that the yuan would remain stable, portfolio inflows would likely continue—and a modest deficit need not put any real strain on China’s reserves

content.text: A managed reset to a lower band would let exporters cut dollar prices and redirect exports elsewhere without losing yuan revenue.
content.reason: Depreciation lets exporters lower foreign prices while keeping domestic-currency margins.

passages.source_excerpt: That would let Chinese firms (who have already started to complain) cut their dollar prices (offsetting some of the impact of the tariff) without reducing their yuan revenues

content.text: Controlled depreciations risk being front-run, as in 2015–16.
content.reason: Predictable currency moves invite speculative outflows that can overshoot.

passages.source_excerpt: Controlled depreciations are hard—the market (even a controlled market like the market for the yuan) obviously has an incentive to front run any predictable move (as China learned in 15 and 16).

content.text: A weaker yuan would drag other Asian currencies down, pressure Turkey-like economies, and hurt European and Japanese exporters.
content.reason: A large exporter's depreciation shifts adjustment onto competitors and export-reliant economies.

passages.source_excerpt: A weaker yuan, in effect, redistributes some of China’s trade pain globally

reasons: boxes: `C4` the name `turkey-like` does not occur in the article

content.text: Depreciation risks provoking Trump into higher or broader tariffs.
content.reason: Offsetting a tariff via currency invites the tariffing party to escalate.

passages.source_excerpt: Trump would also have to decide if he would raise the tariff rate above 25 percent in response to China’s depreciation

content.text: China will likely limit near-term yuan weakness while it tests whether a deal is still possible, saving a major depreciation for after tariffs are fully extended.
content.reason: A player holding a retaliatory option keeps it in reserve while escalation can still be averted.

passages.source_excerpt: That’s why my best guess is that China limits any near-term move as it tries to see if there is still time (and will) to cut a deal that avoids further escalation.

content.text: Exchange rate moves matter as much as tariffs but get far less attention.
content.reason: Currency swings can affect trade and growth more than headline tariff changes.

passages.source_excerpt: The gap between the extensive coverage that trade policy shifts receive relative to the limited coverage typically provided to the impact of exchange rate moves is a pet peeve of mine.
